questions.q: Where is Windows advanced audit policy configured?
options: Local Security Policy (secpol.msc) or, in a domain, Group Policy under Advanced Audit Policy Configuration
Only inside Event Viewer itself
Only through the Sysmon configuration XML file
It cannot be configured — it is fixed at install time
questions.explain: Audit policy lives in Local Security Policy or Group Policy; without the right subcategory enabled there, the matching event never gets generated.

questions.q: Which audit policy category governs Event IDs 4624 and 4625 from Lesson 10?
options: Logon/Logoff
Object Access
Policy Change
Detailed Tracking
questions.explain: Logon/Logoff governs successful and failed logon events, among related session events.

options: Dumps the current audit policy setting for every top-level category
Installs Sysmon with the default configuration
Deletes the entire Security log
Creates a new user account
questions.explain: auditpol is the command-line tool for viewing and setting audit policy, useful for scripting a consistent baseline or confirming what's enabled on a system.

questions.q: What is the real cost of enabling every audit subcategory, especially Object Access across a busy file server?
options: Storage and SIEM-ingestion costs climb fast, and the volume of events can bury the signal that actually matters — alert fatigue
There is no real cost — logging everything is always strictly better
It automatically disables the Security log
It prevents Sysmon from running at all
questions.explain: Logging everything sounds safer but isn't free — a flood of events makes the few that matter harder to find, not easier.

questions.q: What is the consequence of logging too little, such as never enabling Account Management auditing?
options: Events like 4720 and 4728 simply never get generated — there's no record to review after the fact, no matter how good detection logic is
The Security log automatically falls back to Sysmon data instead
Windows generates those events anyway through a different log
It has no real consequence as long as Logon/Logoff auditing is enabled
questions.explain: A gap in audit policy is a gap in evidence — it's discovered only when the missing record is needed most.
